1.0 Ludwig Wittgenstein

1.01 Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (PDF) treats a proposition as a picture of a possible fact. Its saying/showing distinction marks what a factual proposition can state and what its logical form can only display.
1.02 Philosophical Investigations (PDF) follows words into language-games: giving orders, reporting, joking, praying. Use, training, rule-following, and correction give each practice its shape.



1.1 A.J. Ayer & Bertrand Russell.

1.11 Language, Truth and Logic by A. J. Ayer asks whether a proposition is analytic or open to empirical verification. The test is severe enough to make the status of ethical and metaphysical claims itself contentious.
1.12 On Denoting (1905) and Mathematical Logic as Based on the Theory of Types (1908) by Bertrand Russell ask how an expression works in a proposition when its grammatical form misleads us about its logical role.



1.2 Frank Ramsey

1.21 Truth and Probability (1926) connects degrees of belief to the odds a person would accept.
1.22 General Propositions and Causality (1929) calls belief “a map of neighbouring space by which we steer.” The 2025 notes extend that image: much of the map is water, and old beliefs leave marks after a revision.



1.3 The Cluster Structure of Thingspace⁠ by Eliezer Yudkowsky treats categories as clusters of correlated properties, a reason to examine a category’s predictive use instead of searching for its essence.


1.4 On Bounded Distrust by Zvi Mowshowitz asks what signal can still be extracted from a source whose distortions are known. Distrust has to be calibrated to the claim and context.


2.0 Albert Camus

2.01 The Myth of Sisyphus asks whether life is worth living once the demand for meaning meets an indifferent world. Its answer is revolt without an appeal to philosophical suicide.
2.02 The Rebel asks how refusal of injustice can remain committed to human limits, rather than license murder in the name of a promised future.
2.03 The First Man, the unfinished novel about childhood in colonial Algeria, returns the argument to poverty, family, and the search for an origin.

2.1 Gilles Deleuze

2.10 Nietzsche and Philosophy by Gilles Deleuze reads critique through the origin and value of values. This is the route into aesthetic value in the existing Nietzsche notes.
2.11 A Thousand Plateaus (PDF) by Deleuze and Félix Guattari develops rhizomes, assemblages, and multiplicities as ways to describe relations that do not grow from one root.



2.2 Being and Time (PDF) by Martin Heidegger starts from Dasein, already situated in a world of uses and concerns. Readiness-to-hand and presence-at-hand name two ways a thing becomes intelligible in that situation.


2.3 The Sickness unto Death by Søren Kierkegaard and The Need for Roots by Simone Weil hold a question open: what gives a self form when possibility multiplies? Hyperabundance makes that question practical, because chosen commitments need time and attention to become real.


3.0 A notebook and an essay do different work in a writing life.

3.01 On Keeping a Notebook by Joan Didion keeps contact with earlier selves. Its entries record how an event felt to the writer, even when they would make poor evidence for a factual diary.
3.02 The Age of the Essay and Writes and Write-Nots by Paul Graham treat an essay as an attempt (essayer): write a claim down, follow its consequences, and find out where thought is incomplete.



3.1 Henrik Karlsson’s three essays make a sequence from private thought to public discovery to practical agency.

3.1 Henrik Karlsson’s three essays make a sequence from private thought to public discovery to practical agency.

3.11 Writing to Think pins a vague claim to the page so that contradictions and counterexamples become visible. The friction is part of the method.
3.12 A Blog Post Is a Very Long and Complex Search Query treats specific public writing as a way to find people who can answer, challenge, or extend an unusual interest.
3.13 Agentic Fragments uses a reknitted sweater to show agency as seeing more degrees of freedom in an object, then acting on them. The public excerpt ends before the paid essay’s other fragments.



3.2 Impact, Agency, and Taste by Ben Kuhn separates choosing consequential work from carrying it through. Audience of One by Jasmine Sun belongs beside it as a prompt to examine whose judgment shapes taste and where the Overton Window enters the room.


3.3 The tools-for-thought track asks how a computer can extend a person’s working memory and agency.

3.31 As We May Think by Vannevar Bush imagines the memex and its associative trails; The Dream Machine by M. Mitchell Waldrop follows J. C. R. Licklider’s later vision of human-computer symbiosis.
3.32 Magic Ink by Bret Victor, Timeful Texts by Andy Matuschak and Michael Nielsen, and Tufte CSS give the page room for context, interaction, memory, and sidenotes.
3.33 File Over App by Steph Ango puts durable files under the owner’s control. Together these works explain the interest in personal computing and malleable software.



3.4 Universal Love, Said the Cactus Person by Scott Alexander belongs here because its demand for propositional proof interrupts an encounter. The 2025 notes use it to ask whether insisting on verification can turn a subject into an object.

4.0 Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (PDF) by Abelson and Sussman teaches procedures, data, and interpreters by constructing them, then changing the abstraction boundary.

4.01 The Art of Doing Science and Engineering by Richard Hamming makes sustained attention to important problems part of the craft.
4.02 How To Ask Questions The Smart Way by Eric S. Raymond asks for prior investigation and a precise account of the failure. Reading source code is often how a question becomes precise.



4.1 A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948) by Claude Shannon measures information against uncertainty in a distribution. On Exactitude in Science by Jorge Luis Borges supplies the counterimage of a map as large as its empire. Information theory, entropy, and compression matter because a useful representation leaves something out.


5.0 Cinema is a set of recurring questions about time, belonging, and what another person can teach us.

5.01 Past Lives (Celine Song) and Paris, Texas (Wim Wenders) return to lives that might have been and relationships altered by absence.
5.02 Good Will Hunting (Gus Van Sant) and Dead Poets Society (Peter Weir) put education, intimacy, and lived experience beside book knowledge.
5.03 La Haine (Mathieu Kassovitz) and The Defiant Ones (Stanley Kramer) put people in a social conflict they cannot think their way out of alone.
5.04 Tenet (Christopher Nolan) makes time itself the puzzle, then asks what an action means when cause and effect no longer arrive in their usual order.



5.1 Ma Gastronomie by Fernand Point and Marco Pierre White’s craft aphorisms keep cooking close to feeling, timing, and repeated practice. The practical version is a 3-quart Made In stainless clad saucier, Sunday uovo pasta, velouté, and atelier with friends.
